code_label: Quantum computing has reached an intermediate noisy stage
text_span: Quantum computing is no longer in its early stages.
rationale: States the paper’s framing of the field as mature enough for practical study.

code_label: NISQ era defined by insufficient error correction
text_span: there are still not enough qubits to perform quantum error correction, hence the noisy name.
rationale: Defines the central hardware limitation motivating the work.

code_label: QAOA highlighted as a prominent variational algorithm
text_span: variational algorithms gained prominence and, among them, there is one called QAOA
rationale: Identifies QAOA as the algorithmic focus within NISQ computing.

code_label: Study objective is applying QAOA to finance
text_span: The objective of the present work was to apply this algorithm to solve an optimization problem in the finance area known as portfolio optimization.
rationale: Direct statement of the research objective.

code_label: Ideal and noisy simulations were both performed
text_span: This application took place both in an ideal way (without noise) and in a way consistent with the current capacity of quantum computers (with noise).
rationale: Describes the comparative simulation design.

code_label: Qiskit used for simulation and cloud access
text_span: Both were simulated using IBM’s Python tool for simulation and access via cloud of quantum computers called Qiskit.
rationale: Specifies the software platform used.

code_label: Noisy QAOA performed worse but remained satisfactory
text_span: The results suggest that the performance of the QAOA with noise was as expected worse than the ideal case, por´em still satisfactory within the limitations of the method.
rationale: Summarizes the main comparative finding and preserves the hedging language.

code_label: Quantum advantage remains a motivating possibility
text_span: This advantage when using quantum algorithms concerning the classical ones is believed by some to be a property of quantum computation.
rationale: Frames the broader motivation for quantum algorithms.

code_label: QAOA presented as a practical NISQ application
text_span: A practical application for NISQ-era quantum computers in a variational algorithm called QAOA
rationale: Connects the algorithm to the NISQ-era use case.

code_label: Portfolio optimization chosen as the target problem
text_span: The present work goal is to apply this QAOA method to a finance optimization problem called portfolio optimization.
rationale: Restates the specific application domain.

code_label: Qiskit used to compare ideal and noisy cases
text_span: Qiskit will be used to simulate quantum computers with (the NISQ case) and without noise (the ideal case).
rationale: States the comparative simulation approach in the introduction.

code_label: Chapter structure organized around theory, finance, implementation, and conclusion
text_span: The chapter 1 is responsible for introducing quantum computation in its circuit and adiabatic models.
rationale: Shows the paper’s organization and scope across chapters.

code_label: Qubit defined as a two-dimensional Hilbert space
text_span: Mathematically, we say that a qubit is a two-dimensional Hilbert space with states of the form:
rationale: Core conceptual definition used throughout the paper.

code_label: Superposition and normalization introduced as qubit properties
text_span: The main difference between a bit and a qubit is that a bit can only be |0⟩ or |1⟩ while a qubit can be in any linear combination of these two states.
rationale: Explains the quantum property underlying the circuit model.

code_label: Single-qubit gates are unitary operators
text_span: Mathematically, it is a 2 × 2 unitary operator
rationale: Defines the mathematical form of quantum gates.

code_label: Universal gate set can approximate any unitary
text_span: the set of quantum gates: H, S, CNOT, and T can be used to approximately build any unitary operation to arbitrary accuracy.
rationale: States a key computational capability of the gate model.

code_label: Adiabatic computation encodes answers in the ground state
text_span: it consists in evolving a system adiabatically in a way that the problem answer is encoded in the ground state of the system.
rationale: Defines the alternative computation model discussed before QAOA.

code_label: QUBO mapping connects optimization to Ising form
text_span: there is a map connecting the Ising spin-glass Hamiltonian and the cost function of a QUBO problem.
rationale: Establishes the mathematical bridge used later for QAOA.

code_label: Noise modeled as open-system interaction
text_span: In the real world, every quantum mechanical system is an open system which means that they interact with their environment.
rationale: Introduces the paper’s noise framework.

code_label: Quantum channels described by Kraus operators
text_span: These operation elements are important because they are all that is needed to describe noise in a system.
rationale: Identifies the formalism used to model noise.

code_label: Phase damping equivalent to phase flip
text_span: This means that phase damping and phase flip are the same thing.
rationale: Analytical observation about channel equivalence.

code_label: Readout error can misclassify measured bits
text_span: The bit 1 can be read as 0 with some probability p(0|1) and the bit 0 can be read as 1 with other probability p(1|0).
rationale: Defines the measurement error model used in noisy simulations.

code_label: VQA combines quantum circuit and classical optimization
text_span: it is an algorithm where a parameterized quantum circuit runs on a quantum computer to solve the problem and a classical algorithm running on a classical computer optimizes the quantum circuit parameters.
rationale: Describes the hybrid structure of the algorithmic framework.

code_label: Cost function minimum encodes the solution
text_span: A cost function C = C(⃗θ) needs to have the following elements:
rationale: Introduces the optimization objective in VQAs.

code_label: Parameter-shift rule used for gradients
text_span: The gradient of C(⃗θ) can be written with:
rationale: States the gradient-evaluation method discussed for VQAs.

code_label: Barren plateaus cause vanishing gradients
text_span: this phenomenon occurs when the partial derivatives (gradients) magnitude exponentially vanishes with the system size
rationale: Identifies a major optimization difficulty.

code_label: Noise can induce barren plateaus
text_span: Another way to have BP is by introducing noise to the system
rationale: Links noise to training failure in variational circuits.

code_label: QAOA approximates annealing through layered unitaries
text_span: The quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) [31] is a VQA that approximates optimization problem solutions.
rationale: Defines the algorithm at the center of the paper.

code_label: QAOA improves with more layers
text_span: The QAOA approximation improves with the layer number p succeeding in the limit p →∞.
rationale: States the expected convergence behavior of QAOA.

code_label: QAOA parameters are classically optimized
text_span: These (⃗γ, ⃗β) are the parameters to be optimized by the classical computer.
rationale: Specifies the hybrid optimization loop.

code_label: QAOA output is an approximation to the ground state
text_span: This QAOA final state is an approximation to the ground state of Hf because the algorithm approximates the annealing process.
rationale: States the intended meaning of the final state.

code_label: QAOA limitations include exponential parameter cost and noise
text_span: The main restraint to this algorithm is the exponential cost of optimizing the 2p parameters (⃗γ, ⃗β) (NP-hard problem).
rationale: Explicitly states a computational limitation.

code_label: Portfolio theory links return and risk
text_span: The Modern Portfolio Theory was created by Markowitz in [52] and it relates the expected return of a portfolio with its risk.
rationale: Introduces the finance framework used in the application.

code_label: Portfolio optimization seeks best return for given risk
text_span: This theory’s goal is to find which portfolio among the possible has the best return for a given risk.
rationale: States the optimization goal in finance terms.

code_label: Risk quantified through covariance matrix
text_span: A way to quantify this uncertainty about this varying price is to use the covariance matrix:
rationale: Defines the risk measure used in the cost function.

code_label: Sharpe ratio used to compare portfolios
text_span: The quality of a portfolio is measured with the Sharpe ratio, Sr, which quantifies the extra return one receives for the extra volatility one endures for a riskier asset
rationale: Identifies an evaluation metric used in the examples.

code_label: Binary encoding simplifies the problem for quantum computation
text_span: The binary version of the problem is more digestible to quantum computation because the cost function of equation (3.12) turns into a QUBO problem.
rationale: Explains the modeling choice adopted for QAOA.

code_label: Practical example uses Yfinance data over 2016-2023
text_span: As a practical example of portfolio optimization, we utilized the Yfinance package made available by Yahoo! Finance.
rationale: Specifies the data source and example setup.

code_label: Classical efficient frontier identified from random portfolios
text_span: This plot shows the efficient frontier:
rationale: Describes the classical benchmark used for comparison.

code_label: Qiskit Finance provides the implementation framework
text_span: For the present work, the QAOA method was applied using the Qiskit framework.
rationale: States the implementation environment.

code_label: COBYLA chosen as gradient-free optimizer
text_span: For the present work, the classical optimization part of QAOA was done using the constrained optimization by linear approximation (COBYLA) method.
rationale: Specifies the classical optimizer used.

code_label: QAOA circuit alternates mixer and problem unitaries
text_span: the QAOA quantum circuit alternates between the operations UHf(γk) and UH0(βk).
rationale: Describes the circuit structure implemented.

code_label: Noiseless simulations used statevector simulator
text_span: Qiskit’s State vector simulator was used for these simulations.
rationale: Specifies the noiseless simulation backend.

code_label: Two-qubit case with large return gap converged
text_span: As one can see in figure 4.6, QAOA converged to the correct answer (only buy JBSS3).
rationale: Reports successful convergence in the first two-qubit example.

code_label: Small return gap caused failure to converge
text_span: QAOA did not converge to the correct answer (only buy BBAS3), it stuck between the states |10⟩ and |01⟩.
rationale: Reports failure in the second two-qubit example.

code_label: Smaller energy gap associated with closer returns
text_span: one can see that there is a smaller energy gap between the ground state and the first excited state when the expected returns are closer to each other.
rationale: Analytical observation linking problem structure to spectral gap.

code_label: Three-qubit case converged to the correct answer
text_span: As one can see in figure 4.10, QAOA converged to the correct answer (buy EMBR3 and JBSS3).
rationale: Reports success in the three-qubit noiseless simulation.

code_label: Four-qubit case converged to the correct answer
text_span: As one can see in figure 4.11, QAOA converged to the correct answer (buy BRKM5 and VALE3).
rationale: Reports success in the four-qubit noiseless simulation.

code_label: Five-qubit case did not quite converge but remained informative
text_span: QAOA did not quite converge to the correct answer (buy BBSE3 and CIEL3).
rationale: Reports the mixed outcome in the five-qubit noiseless simulation.

code_label: Five-qubit anomaly may relate to state count
text_span: It may have something to do with the large number of states (32 states)
rationale: States a possible explanation with explicit uncertainty.

code_label: Noisy simulations used IBM Manila model
text_span: they used the same noisy model as one of the IBM quantum machines.
rationale: Specifies the noisy backend used for comparison.

code_label: Noisy model includes depolarizing, thermal relaxation, and readout errors
text_span: The noisy model of Ibmq manila and Ibmq lima consists of a depolarizing channel for single and two-qubit operations followed by a thermal relaxation error
rationale: Summarizes the noise model composition.

code_label: Noisy two-qubit results were worse than noiseless but still above random
text_span: the noisy case is worse than the noiseless case as expected.
rationale: Summarizes the first noisy comparison outcome.

code_label: Noise introduced penalized states into the distribution
text_span: the penalized states, |11⟩ and |00⟩, show up in the probability distribution due to the noise.
rationale: Explains why noisy energy convergence degraded.

code_label: Noisy small-gap case underperformed random guessing
text_span: the green line is below the cyan which means that a random guess is better than using QAOA.
rationale: Reports a particularly poor noisy outcome.

code_label: Noisy three-qubit case remained better than random
text_span: The green line stays above the cyan line, meaning the noisy simulation is better than a random guess.
rationale: Reports the noisy three-qubit performance.

code_label: Lima noise model performed better than Manila
text_span: one can notice that the Lima machine noisy model return better results than the Manila noisy model.
rationale: Compares two noisy hardware models.

code_label: Difference may be due to T2
text_span: The reason for this may be due to the difference in the T2 parameters (phase damping).
rationale: Provides a tentative explanation with hedging.

code_label: Real IBM hardware was impractical for the study
text_span: they were not viable.
rationale: States a practical limitation of running on actual devices.

code_label: Queueing and calibration make real-device runs too slow
text_span: Trying to use the same methodology seen in 4.4 for the four qubit case for example, 16380 queues would be needed
rationale: Explains why real hardware was not used.

code_label: QAOA results are satisfactory within current limitations
text_span: the behavior of QAOA in solving the portfolio optimization problem is satisfactory for the two, three, and four-qubit cases within the energy problem restriction.
rationale: Summarizes the main conclusion for the smaller cases.

code_label: Noise worsens performance as expected
text_span: The noisy case showed that the expectation value of energy is not a good parameter to analyze the QAOA performance due to the emergence of the penalized states
rationale: Highlights a key interpretive conclusion from the noisy runs.

code_label: Five-qubit case remains unexplained
text_span: The five-qubit case was an outlier and the reason for this is not clear as discussed in the previous chapter.
rationale: States an unresolved anomaly.

code_label: Future work includes warm-starting and mixed Hamiltonians
text_span: it is possible to test QAOA modifications like the warm-starting technique or the mixed Hamiltonian technique to see if they can improve the results seen in the present work.
rationale: Explicit future research direction.

code_label: Future work includes a six-qubit simulation
text_span: A simulation with six qubits could help understand the results seen from the five-qubit simulation.
rationale: Proposes a next-step experiment.

code_label: Future work could use a new probability-gap metric
text_span: The adoption of a new parameter based on the difference between the probability of the optimal state and the probability of the second most probable state
rationale: Suggests a new evaluation metric.

code_label: Future work may encode weights with more qubits
text_span: Instead of using this binary weight vector, one could add more qubits and encode the probabilities of the weight vector
rationale: Proposes a more precise encoding approach.

code_label: Error mitigation may improve noisy results
text_span: IBM, for example, is studying error mitigation techniques to reduce the effect of noise on its machine’s results.
rationale: Identifies a prospective technical improvement.
